Scientifically (statistically) speaking, you can. Falsification is the premise which underlies all modern science. I didn't explain it in detail above as it wasn't relevant, but I'm happy to discuss.

From what I gathered, falsification is based on a group of theories that disproves an idea. When enough theories are proven, then the counter point is declared completely false even without having to directly prove it. Is that the gist of it?

Effectively, yes. I was thinking more about it, and what you said before is certainly true from a perspective. There's the classic falsification example of "all swans are white", which can't be categorically proven without examining all swans. Frequently, though, we don't have the ability to do this, so we select and test a sample, come to a conclusion, and calculate the probability that our conclusion is wrong (p-value). Most scientists will accept a hypothesis as verified if the probability that it is wrong is less than 5% (termed 'statistically significant').

Technically, it's a bit messier than this. What we really are doing is creating a series of counter-claims to our hypothesis (termed 'null hypotheses') and testing the probability that these are correct, then applying a statistical adaptation of reductio ad absurdum to argue that if the null hypotheses can't be verified, their collective counter-claim (our hypothesis) is by nature true. If you're trying to prove something doesn't exist (let's say a correlation between cholesterol consumption and coronary disease), you'll often try to prove that it does exist and hope to find no association/correlation. Again, as you pointed out, this really isn't proof per se that something doesn't exist, so much as a probabilistic declaration that it is unlikely.
